title: Distributional statistics of nonequilibrium
authors: Harrison Hartle, Aanjaneya Kumar, David H. Wolpert
abstract: We establish a reference modeling framework for random probability distributions subject to constraints. Generalizing the hyperensemble approach of Crooks, we formulate Jaynesian priors of maximal uncertainty over the unit simplex of categorical distributions. This framework is entirely general, but we primarily investigate models with constraints on physically relevant quantities, namely, average energy and Shannon entropy. A constraint on the exact value of average energy uniquely determines a Boltzmann-Gibbs equilibrium, but also defines a hyperplanar subset of the probability simplex consisting of all distributions with that value of average energy. The associated hyperensemble has a uniform probability density across all such distributions, regardless of distance to equilibrium. Such reference models make predictions of generic nonequilibrium properties such as the mean and modal microstate distributions and the expected free energy of a random distribution, which we examine analytically and via exact sampling algorithms. Moreover, introducing constraints on Shannon entropy permits parametric access to tunably nonequilibrium regimes. The approach follows conventional Jaynesian modeling logic and is compatible with standard Bayesian inference, and reduces to Boltzmann-Gibbs statistics when Shannon entropy is maximized. We examine the physical predictions of this scheme, and demonstrate its wide compatibility with other approaches to nonequilibrium modeling. We illustrate the framework in three scenarios: (i) comparison to superstatistics quasi-equilibrium modeling, (ii) generation of random nonequilibrium steady states, and (iii) Bayesian inference under a prior hyperensemble. We highlight numerous prospects for theoretical extensions and empirical application.
summary: This paper develops a general hyperensemble framework to model uncertainty over probability distributions constrained by physical quantities like energy or entropy. It generalizes existing methods by using maximum entropy principles at the hyperensemble level. The framework predicts equilibrium states and allows for the rigorous description of tunable, non-equilibrium statistical regimes.
main_problem: The paper establishes a general reference modeling framework for determining the probability density over possible probability distributions (a hyperensemble) when only constraints on physical quantities are known.
main_result: The framework shows that imposing constraints on average energy uniquely determines the Boltzmann-Gibbs equilibrium, while allowing for tunable nonequilibrium regimes by constraining Shannon entropy.
method: The core method involves maximizing the differential entropy of the hyperensemble subject to various constraints (e.g., fixed average energy or fixed entropy), following Jaynesian model selection logic.
model_or_system: The model concerns probability distributions $p$ over a finite set of microstates $X$, where the uncertainty is modeled by a prior probability density $P(p)$ over the unit simplex $\Delta(X)$.
key_observables: Shannon entropy $S(p)$, average energy $E(p)$, and the Kullback-Leibler divergence $D(p||\pi_ eta)$.
important_parameters: The inverse temperature parameter $ eta$, and the constraint parameters $\gamma$ (for energy) and $\alpha$ (for entropy).
main_assumptions: The framework assumes the ability to define and sample from the hyperensemble $P(p)$ based on imposed constraints, which are treated as exact or expected values.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the mathematical forms of various hyperensembles ($P(p)$) based on energy and entropy constraints, and show the limiting behavior of divergence measures in extreme temperature regimes.
paper_structure: The paper develops the general framework by defining the hyperensemble $P(p)$, deriving the mathematical forms for energy-constrained and entropy-constrained ensembles, and then analyzing the physical predictions and limiting behaviors (e.g., $ eta 	o 0$ and $ eta 	o \infty$).
why_interesting: The rigorous mathematical treatment of epistemic uncertainty in statistical mechanics, especially the generalization of the ensemble concept to a hyperensemble, provides powerful tools for modeling non-equilibrium steady states beyond standard equilibrium assumptions.
